protections: P1 (inferred, not tied to the advisory text): the artifact-repository location and its secret references must come from a source the workflow author cannot forge (the controller-resolved ref), not from caller-writable Workflow status
P2 (inferred): stored artifact credentials must only be resolved and sent to the artifact repository the workflow was actually given, not to a location that the caller embeds in an artifact

traps.reason_to_dismiss: status.artifactRepositoryRef is written by the controller, so it looks trusted
the server only reads what the controller already resolved
a workflow author can already mount any secret in the namespace, so resolving an artifact's own secret refs adds nothing
GC pods only delete objects, so they seem harmless
falling back to the controller-namespace config map is a tested feature
template volumes may name any secret anyway, so a podSpecPatch mount adds no new reach

conflicts.what: a natural T1 fix (only trust controller-resolved refs, or force the ref namespace to the workflow namespace) breaks the tested controller-namespace fallback (artifactrepositories_test.go:52-77) unless that namespace stays explicitly allowed

making the server refuse artifacts that carry their own location breaks case 1 (artifact-defined location, artifact_server.go:405-410,435) that legitimate workflows use for explicit input and output locations

fairness_risks: Artifacts that declare their own full location and secret refs are a documented must-keep-working shape (artifact_server.go:405-410); a rule refusing them would contradict legitimate use
The controller-namespace fallback for artifactRepositoryRef is pinned by a unit test (artifactrepositories_test.go:52); a rule limiting refs to the workflow namespace would break it
Workflow status is not a subresource (argoproj.io_workflows.yaml:55); a rule ignoring a pre-set status would also affect legitimate re-creation and resubmission flows that carry status (unverified)

design.why: If the advisories turn out to match these surfaces, this is the best design. T1/T2 (forged status ref, one guard in artifactrepositories.get), T3 (server resolves secrets for an artifact-chosen location) and T4 (GC pod mounts secrets named in status) are independent. Each has a different reason to dismiss: controller-written status, a namespace author's existing secret access, and delete-only pods. T5 adds the mimo-type coupled value, the tested controller-namespace fallback. Marked unusable because neither advisory's mechanism could be tied to pinned code.

unverified: The exact mechanism of GHSA-c2hv-4pfj-mm2r / CVE-2025-62157 and GHSA-7vf8-2cr6-54mf: no advisory text was available, and no code in the pinned tree is recognisably the A fix (no redaction or credential-masking code exists: searches for redact/mask/sanitize found nothing relevant)

Whether A's fix commits 18ad5138b6bc / bded09fe4abd are in the pinned history: git objects outside the worktree could not be read under the tool restriction. HEAD 'Merge commit from fork' does contain the CVE-2025-62156 zip-slip guard (workflow/executor/executor.go:948-957)

That T1-T6 are the routes the advisories describe: they are code-verified places where credential-bearing repository config or secret refs come from caller-writable input, but none is confirmed as A's or B's route
Whether the Workflow API server or an admission path strips user-supplied status on create: no stripping was found by grep, but it was not traced end to end

Whether the pod-informer diff log (workflow/controller/pod/controller.go:94, util/diff/diff.go:11-17, debug-gated) or the offloaded ARGO_TEMPLATE config map (workflow/controller/workflowpod.go:448-477) is the leak route: both carry only secret references in the code read here
Dependency-bump history: not determinable from the worktree
